B: Alright. Can you hear me okay?
A: Yes, I can, thank you. Can you hear me? Sorry, my laptop's a bit old.
B: Yeah, you're fine. I'm Darren.
A: Leanne. Nice to meet you.
B: You too. Where are you, then?
A: Walsall, in the West Midlands. Erm, and you?
B: Taunton. Somerset.
A: Oh, lovely. I've driven past it on the way to Devon, I think. On the M5.
B: Most people have. That's about all we're known for, the M5. What do you do?
A: I'm a practice nurse at a GP surgery. I run the asthma and diabetes clinics, and I do smears and baby immunisations. Four days a week.
B: Right. Busy, I'd imagine.
A: It is, yes. Monday mornings the phone lines are a nightmare, you can hear the receptionists sighing from the other end of the corridor. Sorry, what about you?
B: Duty manager at a leisure centre. Pool, gym, sports hall. I run the shifts, lifeguards, reception, sort the rota out when someone rings in sick. And I look after the pool plant, the chlorine, water testing, that sort of thing.
A: Oh, that's funny. I've just been talking to a girl who's a lifeguard. Ellie, I think she's in our group.
B: Is she? Whereabouts?
A: North Devon. Barnstaple. She was telling me about a rescue she did. She was very matter-of-fact about it, but you could tell it had stayed with her, you know.
B: Yeah. It does. You train for it, you do it, and then you go home and have your dinner. I've had a few over the years. You don't dwell on it, I find. That's about it really.
A: No. I think that's probably sensible. I'm not very good at not dwelling, if I'm honest. I lie awake going over things I said to patients.
B: Everyone's different, I s'pose. You sound like you take care over it, though. That's not a bad thing in a nurse.
A: That's kind. Erm, is the pool busy at the moment?
B: It is now. We were shut two days last week, the boiler went. You've never seen people so cross about not doing their lengths.
A: Oh dear. I can imagine. Do you swim yourself?
B: Few lengths before or after a shift, yeah. And five-a-side Thursdays. Walk the dog along the canal of an evening.
A: Oh, I walk along the canal most evenings. The towpath. Not with a dog, though, I just borrow next door's cat for company. Well, she sits on my wheelie bin and watches me go.
B: Ha. That's still company.
A: It is, I suppose. What's your dog called?
B: Pip. Jack Russell cross. She's getting on a bit now, going a bit deaf. I shout her and she just carries on sniffing a hedge.
A: Bless her. Is she alright otherwise?
B: Yeah, she's fine. Selective hearing, Claire reckons. That's my partner. She says I've got the same thing.
A: Sorry, I haven't asked you anything very interesting. I'm not very good at this sort of thing, starting off.
B: You're doing alright. Better than the last one, to be honest. Two Darrens, both from Taunton, we just talked about dogs and cricket.
A: Oh, really? Both from Taunton?
